uncited: This article defines the mathematical framework for transforming 3D Gaussian primitives from world space into the 2D image plane for rasterization in 3D Gaussian Splatting.
It solves the problem of accurately projecting 3D ellipsoids onto a 2D sensor plane while preserving geometric fidelity and enabling differentiable rendering.

It sets apart from standard perspective projection by supporting optimal tangent-plane projections [3293-optimal-gaussian-splatting.md] and specialized geometries such as cone-beam X-ray scanning [3458-3d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization-cone-beam-scanner-space.md].

All methods in this family share the core objective of mapping a 3D Gaussian primitive, defined by mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, to a 2D Gaussian distribution suitable for alpha blending or density summation.

**World-to-Camera/Scanner Transformation:** Transforming the primitive's mean and covariance into a local coordinate system where the viewing direction is aligned with a principal axis (typically the z-axis).
**Projection:** Mapping the 3D geometry to a 2D plane.
This can be a standard perspective projection, an optimal tangent-plane projection, or a ray-space integration for non-standard geometries.
**Covariance Handling:** Computing the 2D covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2D}$ from the 3D covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}'$ in the local space.
This often involves a Jacobian matrix $\mathbf{J}$ of the projection function: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2D} \approx \mathbf{J} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}' \mathbf{J}^\top$.
**Rasterization:** Evaluating the 2D Gaussian at pixel coordinates to determine opacity or density contribution.
Adapts the rasterization projection for panoramic images by mapping pixel coordinates to the unit sphere using equisolid angle or similar projection models.
The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting method [17] uses a fixed perspective projection plane.
